name: Vinaceous-Lilac
lede: Vinaceous-Lilac is a soft, dusty mauve-pink, Robert Ridgway's 1912 pairing of his wine-tinged "vinaceous" naming scheme with the color of the lilac flower.

sections.title: A wine-tinted lilac
sections.body:
Ridgway plated this hue in 1912 at plate XLIV, hue 69''', tone b; the ISCC-NBS system later filed it as block 251, a light greyish purplish red [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[anemone]], [[grey-pink]], [[candida]] and [[rosy-brown]], at 2.6, 3.3, 
In our library it is an exact color match to [[mauve-rose]] (CIEDE2000 0.0), with ISCC-NBS alternate names Intimate Mood and Mauve Orchid filed in the same block [2]. Its nearest distinct neighbor is [[anemone]], almost the same at a distance of 2.6, with [[grey-pink]] close behind [2]. Measured in LCH it is lightness 62, chroma 18 and hue 360 degrees, a pale, greyed red-purple [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this mauve-pink in only 29 of 23,781 paintings (0.12%, as photographed), rarer than 63% of the named colors we track [3]. It most often plays a hidden color, found this way in 62% of its 16 strongest matches [3]. The earliest dated match is Bartolomeo Caporali's work from 1452, with 21 dated paintings in all running to 1917; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [3]. That is 460 years before Ridgway's own 1912 record, so the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the pigment was there [3].

origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature
